# Epic Games Lawsuit: Every Fortnite Case and Who Actually Gets Paid

**Active Litigation**

As of September 30, 2026, the only Epic Games settlement paying U.S. players that we track is the FTC’s Fortnite refund — and its claims closed on July 9, 2025. A third payment round is still promised for 2026, with no date. The “Epic Games class action” in the September 2026 headlines is a claim by a Dutch foundation on behalf of Dutch players. Epic’s fights with Apple and Google are business cases with no consumer payout, and the Apple case is now before the U.S. Supreme Court.

## Five Different Fights Under One Name

“Epic Games lawsuit” covers cases that have almost nothing in common except Fortnite.  
  
**1. The FTC case (2022).** According to the FTC, Epic used design tricks known as **dark patterns** to charge players for purchases they did not want, let children run up charges without a parent’s permission, and locked some accounts after players disputed charges. Separately, the FTC alleged that Epic collected personal information from children under 13 without parental consent. Epic agreed to pay **$520 million**: a **$245 million** refund order and a **$275 million** COPPA penalty. Only the $245 million pays players.  
  
**2. Epic v. Apple.** Apple and Google both removed Fortnite from their app stores on August 13, 2020, after Epic changed how players could buy V-Bucks, and Epic sued. Epic largely lost against Apple, but a 2021 ruling barred Apple from stopping developers from pointing users to other ways to pay. In April 2025 the trial judge found Apple had violated that order.  
  
**3. Epic v. Google.** A jury sided with Epic in December 2023, finding Google’s Play Store practices anticompetitive.  
  
**4. Player class actions.** In March 2025, two parents filed a proposed U.S. class action alleging that Fortnite’s Item Shop countdown timers were deceptive. In September 2026 a Dutch foundation began a mass claim on behalf of young Dutch players.  
  
**5. Addiction lawsuits.** Families have filed personal-injury suits alleging that popular games, Fortnite among them, were designed to be addictive for children. Every claim above is an allegation unless a court has ruled on it.

### Case details

**FTC refunds:** a **$245 million** FTC administrative order, finalized in March 2023. The refund administrator is Rust Consulting, reachable at 1-833-915-0880. The **$275 million** COPPA penalty came through a separate federal court order filed by the Department of Justice.  
  
**Apple:** *Epic Games, Inc. v. Apple Inc.*, No. 4:20-cv-05640-YGR, U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. Ninth Circuit No. 25-2935, decided December 11, 2025. U.S. Supreme Court No. 25-1311, *Apple Inc. v. Epic Games, Inc.*, on the [Supreme Court docket](https://www.supremecourt.gov/search.aspx?filename=/docket/docketfiles/html/public/25-1311.html).  
  
**Google:** *Epic Games, Inc. v. Google LLC*, No. 3:20-cv-05671-JD, Northern District of California, Judge James Donato, coordinated with *In re Google Play Store Antitrust Litigation*, No. 3:21-md-02981-JD. Ninth Circuit No. 24-6256, decided July 31, 2025.  
  
**Netherlands:** the claim is brought by Stichting Massaschade & Consument (SMC), which says it will go to court if talks with Epic fail.

## Status on September 30, 2026: Nothing New to File

**Fortnite refunds — waiting for round 3.** Claims closed **July 9, 2025**. In June 2025 the FTC sent **969,173 payments totaling more than $126 million**. Its page still says: “We expect to send additional payments in 2026 after we have reviewed and validated all claims.” As of September 30, 2026 it gives no date and still carries a July 2025 date stamp. If you filed after February 14, 2025, the FTC says you do not need to do anything else right now while it reviews claims. Full details: [our Fortnite refund page](/fortnite-ftc-refund) and [our report on the delayed third round](/news/fortnite-ftc-refund-third-round-408-days-after-claims-closed).  
  
**Apple — at the Supreme Court.** On December 11, 2025 the Ninth Circuit upheld the contempt finding but reversed parts of the sanctions, including the outright ban on any Apple commission on purchases made through outside links. On **June 30, 2026** the Supreme Court agreed to hear Apple’s appeal, limited to one question about contempt. Apple filed its brief on September 14; Epic’s is due **November 13, 2026**. No argument date appears on the docket yet. On August 13, 2026, Justice Kagan refused Apple’s request to pause the trial court proceedings.  
  
**Google — verdict stands, deal withdrawn.** The Ninth Circuit affirmed the verdict and injunction on July 31, 2025, and the Supreme Court let the order take effect in October 2025. A settlement announced in November 2025 and revised in March 2026 needed Judge Donato’s approval; according to Gizmodo, Google and Epic withdrew it in July 2026 after the judge voiced skepticism. In August 2026, Aptoide Games became the first rival app store offered inside Google Play in the U.S.  
  
**Player lawsuits.** The Dutch claim is at the demand stage: SMC served Epic with a notice of liability and offered to negotiate. For the U.S. Item Shop timer suit and the addiction suits, we found no settlement and no claim form.

## Which Case Could Involve You

**FTC refund:** it covered players charged in-game currency for items they did not want (January 2017 to September 2022), parents whose child made charges to their card without their knowledge (January 2017 to November 2018), and players whose accounts were locked after disputing charges (January 2017 to September 2022). It only helps you now if you **filed by July 9, 2025**. No new claims are accepted.  
  
**Apple and Google cases:** you are not a party and cannot join. Their outcome changes how app stores handle payment links, fees and rival stores. It does not send money to players. The **$700 million Google Play settlement** is a different case brought by the states, and it pays automatically: see [our Google lawsuit guide](/google-lawsuit).  
  
**Dutch claim:** SMC represents Dutch players who played Fortnite before age 21. It does not cover U.S. players.  
  
**U.S. Item Shop suit and addiction suits:** there is nothing to sign up for. The addiction cases are individual personal-injury suits, not a fund you join; a class action includes you automatically if a class is ever certified or a settlement is reached, and notice would come from a court-appointed administrator.

## What Anyone Has Actually Been Paid

**FTC refunds — the only real money so far.** Round 1 in December 2024 averaged about **$114** per payment; round 2 in June 2025 works out to roughly **$130**. The FTC describes the total sent as “nearly $200 million.” It has not published an amount for round 3, and says each payment depends on factors including how many people filed. Checks must be cashed within 90 days and PayPal payments accepted within 30 days.  
  
**The $275 million COPPA penalty** is a civil penalty, not a refund fund. No player or parent receives any of it.  
  
**Apple and Google cases:** no money for consumers. They are about app store rules.  
  
**Dutch claim:** SMC seeks over **€100 million** in refunds and damages for Dutch players. Nothing has been agreed or awarded.  
  
**U.S. Item Shop suit and addiction suits:** no settlement, no fund, no claim form. Any dollar figure you see attached to them is a guess.

### How cases like this one end

Our copy of the federal courts’ own case database covers 6,924antitrust casesclosed in U.S. federal district courts between 2015and 2026, 37.3% of them filed as class actions:

* •**19.1%** ended in a settlement recorded by the court. Another 14.5% were dismissed voluntarily, which often follows a private settlement — so the real settlement share sits between 19.1% and 33.6%.
* •**11.4%** were decided on a motion before any trial.
* •**1 in 119** reached a trial (0.8%), after a median of 37.1 months.
* •Median time from filing to the end of the case: **11.9 months**.
* •Almost none record a money award in this data (33 of 6,924), and the recorded figures are capped, so we do not publish an average.

These are base rates for this type of case(federal antitrust cases)— not a prediction about this lawsuit, and not legal advice. Source: Federal Judicial Center, Integrated Database (civil), analysed by Settlement Insight. Cases heard in state courts are not included.

## Epic Games Lawsuits Timeline

1. ### August 13, 2020 — Fortnite Pulled From Both App Stores

   Apple and Google remove Fortnite after Epic changes how players can buy V-Bucks. Epic sues both companies.
2. ### December 2022 — $520 Million FTC Settlement

   Epic agrees to a $245 million refund order over dark patterns and a $275 million COPPA penalty. The refund order is finalized in March 2023.
3. ### December 11, 2023 — Jury Rules for Epic Against Google

   The jury finds for Epic on all eleven counts. In October 2024 Judge Donato orders Google to allow rival app stores on Android.
4. ### April 30, 2025 — Apple Held in Contempt

   Judge Gonzalez Rogers finds Apple violated her 2021 injunction, including by charging a 27% commission on linked-out purchases. Fortnite returns to the U.S. App Store on May 20, 2025.
5. ### July 2025 — Refund Claims Close, Google Loses Appeal

   The last day to file a Fortnite refund claim is July 9, 2025. On July 31, 2025 the Ninth Circuit affirms the verdict against Google.
6. ### June 30, 2026 — Supreme Court Takes Apple’s Appeal

   After the Ninth Circuit largely upheld the contempt finding on December 11, 2025, the Supreme Court agrees to hear one contempt question. Epic’s brief is due November 13, 2026; refund round 3 is still pending.

## Three Things to Watch For

A famous brand, young players and a refund that has been “coming in 2026” for over a year is a combination scammers exploit:

“Join the Epic Games class action” ads

The class action in the September 2026 news is Dutch and covers only Dutch players. There is no U.S. claim form for it. A site asking for your Epic login, card number or a fee to “join” is collecting data, not filing anything.

“Your Fortnite round 3 refund is ready” messages

Claims closed July 9, 2025, so any invitation to file one now is fake. Real payments go only to people who already filed, as a check or PayPal payment. The FTC never demands money; the refund administrator’s number is 1-833-915-0880.

Free V-Bucks or an “App Store refund” from the court cases

FTC refunds are paid in real money, not V-Bucks. The Apple and Google cases pay no consumer anything, so a message offering you a share of an Apple or Google ruling is invented.

## Epic Games Lawsuits: Questions People Actually Ask

Short answers to the questions people ask most about this case.

Is there an Epic Games settlement I can file a claim for right now?

No. The FTC’s Fortnite refund stopped taking claims on July 9, 2025, and none of the other cases has a settlement fund or a claim form as of September 30, 2026. For settlements that are open, see [our list of open class action settlements](/open-class-action-settlements).

When is the third Fortnite refund round?

The FTC says it expects to send additional payments in 2026 once all claims are validated. As of September 30, 2026 it has announced no date and no amount. The [FTC refund page](https://www.ftc.gov/enforcement/refunds/fortnite-refunds) is the only authoritative source; our [Fortnite refund page](/fortnite-ftc-refund) tracks it.

What is the Epic Games lawsuit in the news in September 2026?

A Dutch consumer foundation, Stichting Massaschade & Consument, is seeking over €100 million for Dutch players who played Fortnite before age 21. It points to the Dutch regulator’s 2024 fine of €1,125,000 over Item Shop pressure tactics, which a Rotterdam court upheld in January 2026. Epic says the Item Shop has no timer and that parents can require a PIN for purchases. The claim does not include U.S. players.

What is the Supreme Court deciding in Apple v. Epic Games?

Only whether a court may hold a party in civil contempt for violating an injunction’s “spirit” when the order is silent about the conduct. It is not re-deciding whether Apple is a monopoly, and no money for users is at stake. The United States filed a brief supporting neither side on September 21, 2026.

Did Epic Games win its lawsuit against Google?

Yes. The jury ruled for Epic in December 2023, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed on July 31, 2025. The case produced app store changes, not payments to players. The separate $700 million Google Play consumer settlement is explained in [our Google lawsuit guide](/google-lawsuit).

Is there a Fortnite addiction lawsuit?

Families have filed individual lawsuits alleging that video games were designed to addict children, and Epic is named in some, including a Los Angeles Superior Court case filed April 8, 2025. A federal MDL was denied in June 2024 and again on December 10, 2025. We found no settlement. Related cases: [Minecraft](/minecraft-lawsuit) and [Roblox](/roblox-lawsuit).

Does the $275 million COPPA penalty pay parents?

No. It is a civil penalty for alleged children’s-privacy violations. According to the FTC, the settlement also required Epic to turn voice and text chat off by default for children and teens. Only the separate $245 million refund order pays players.

Is there a lawsuit over Fortnite Item Shop timers?

Yes. In March 2025 two parents filed a proposed class action in a San Francisco court, alleging the countdown timers created fake urgency. Epic said the complaint “contains factual errors” and that it would fight the claims. We could not confirm its current status; no settlement has been announced.

# Adobe FTC Lawsuit: 2026 Settlement Explained

•[News](/c/news)•[Gabriel E. Hall](/author/gabriel-e-hall)

![Adobe FTC Lawsuit: 2026 Settlement Explained](/pic/w3840q75/uploads/wp/news/adobe-targeted-by-ftc-due-to-decetive-sub-cancellation-practices-copy_en.jpg.webp)

Adobe agreed to a $150 million settlement in March 2026 over its hidden cancellation fee. What the FTC case alleged, what changed and what to check.

At a glance

* [Adobe and the FTC in 2026: the short answer](#adobe-and-the-ftc-in-2026-the-short-answer)

## Adobe and the FTC in 2026: the short answer

The FTC case against Adobe ended in a settlement. On March 13, 2026 the Justice Department announced that Adobe agreed to pay $75 million in civil penalties and offer customers $75 million in free services, a total of $150 million, to resolve claims that it hid an early termination fee and made cancelling hard.[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement)[[8]](#reuters-adobe-settlement-2026) Adobe said it disagrees with the government's claims and denies any wrongdoing.[[8]](#reuters-adobe-settlement-2026)

The deal comes as a proposed stipulated order that still needs a court to enter it, according to the Justice Department.[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement) We found no later page that says whether the court has entered it, so check the case docket if you need the final status. The case also named two Adobe executives, Maninder Sawhney and David Wadhwani, and the same order is meant to resolve the claims against them.[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement)

Adobe and the FTC case at a glance| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| What was alleged | Hiding the early termination fee (ETF) and making cancellation hard, a violation of ROSCA[[1]](#cite-ftc-1)[[2]](#cite-ftc-2) |
| The ETF | 50 percent of the remaining monthly payments if you cancel in the first year of an annual plan paid monthly[[2]](#cite-ftc-2) |
| Outcome | Proposed settlement announced March 13, 2026[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement) |
| Money | $75 million civil penalty plus $75 million in free services[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement) |
| Adobe's position | Disagrees with the claims and denies wrongdoing[[8]](#reuters-adobe-settlement-2026) |
| Court | U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement) |

## Timeline: from Figma to a $150 million settlement

![Timeline of the Adobe FTC case from the September 2022 Figma deal and the 2023 breakup fee to the 2024 complaint and the March 2026 settlement of 150 million dollars](/pic/w1080q75/uploads/news/adobe-ftc-ftc-lawsuit-timeline-2026.png.webp "Timeline of the Adobe subscription case, 2022 to 2026")

Timeline of the Adobe subscription case, 2022 to 2026. Sources: The Verge, Variety, FTC, Justice Department, Reuters.

Dated events in the Adobe case| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| September 15, 2022 | The Verge reports Adobe will buy Figma in a deal worth $20 billion[[5]](#cite-the-verge-5) |
| Late 2023 | Adobe drops the Figma bid citing regulatory opposition and pays a $1 billion breakup fee[[6]](#cite-variety-6) |
| June 2024 | The FTC takes action against Adobe and two executives over the hidden ETF and cancellation process[[2]](#cite-ftc-2) |
| June 2024 | Adobe publishes a statement responding to the complaint[[4]](#cite-adobe-4) |
| March 13, 2026 | The Justice Department announces the $150 million settlement and injunction[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement) |

## What changed since 2024

In 2024 this was an allegation. The 2024 complaint said Adobe showed the monthly price clearly but buried the ETF in fine print and behind small icons.[[2]](#cite-ftc-2) Now there is a negotiated outcome, with money and rules attached.

The Justice Department says the order requires Adobe to give subscribers easy ways to cancel. Adobe must also clearly disclose any ETF and how it is calculated before enrolling customers. It must remind customers before a free trial longer than seven days turns into a paid plan with an ETF.[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement)

Reuters reports that Adobe said it was pleased to resolve the matter while denying wrongdoing.[[8]](#reuters-adobe-settlement-2026) Nothing in the sources we read says Adobe admitted fault. Our original report below describes the complaint as filed in 2024 and is kept unchanged.

## Risks around subscription traps (our analysis)

Our analysis is that the Adobe case is a pattern, and the same traps appear in many apps. Watch for these.

* **Plans that look monthly but are annual.** The headline price says monthly while the contract runs for a year, as the FTC described.[[2]](#cite-ftc-2)
* **Cancellation fees in small print.** Look for an early termination fee line before you press buy and note how it is calculated.
* **Free trials that turn paid.** The settlement terms include a reminder before a long trial converts to a paid plan with an ETF.[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement) Set your own calendar reminder anyway.
* **Fake cancellation or refund pages.** Scammers imitate subscription support and ask for card details. Always cancel from the official account page and read our [phishing report guide](/how-to/report-phishing).

## Steps if you have an Adobe or similar subscription

![Six steps for software subscribers: read the plan terms, check the fee, set a trial reminder, cancel from the account page, keep proof, watch card statements](/pic/w1080q75/uploads/news/adobe-ftc-ftc-lawsuit-steps-2026.png.webp "Six steps to avoid subscription traps")

Six steps to avoid subscription traps. 2-Spyware, 2026.

**1. Read the plan type.** Check whether a monthly price hides a year-long commitment. Adobe's own page explains its subscription terms and refund policy.[[3]](#cite-adobe-3)

**2. Find the fee.** Look for any early termination fee. In the FTC complaint, it was 50 percent of the remaining monthly payments when cancelling in year one.[[2]](#cite-ftc-2)

**3. Set a trial reminder.** Put the end date of any free trial in your calendar. Do not rely on the company to remind you.

**4. Cancel in your account.** Use the company's own account page. Do not follow links from emails or ads that claim to cancel for you.

**5. Keep proof.** Save the cancellation confirmation email and take screenshots of each page.

**6. Watch your statements.** If billing continues after you cancelled, contact the company in writing and then your card issuer. You can also check if your email was exposed with our [leak check](/check).

## What is still unknown

* Whether the court has entered the proposed order. We found no confirmation after March 13, 2026.
* How customers will receive the $75 million in free services. The pages we read do not describe the process.
* Whether other subscription companies face similar cases. We found nothing we could confirm.

## Our original 2024 report

The text below is our report as first published in 2024. We keep it unchanged for the record; the sections above bring it up to date.

Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has filed a complaint[[1]](#cite-ftc-1) against Adobe and two of its executives, Maninder Sawhney and David Wadhwani, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California.

The complaint accuses Adobe of deceptive practices related to its subscription plans, specifically failing to disclose early termination fees (ETFs) and making the cancellation process unnecessarily complicated.[[2]](#cite-ftc-2)

FTC alleges that these practices violate the Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act (ROSCA), which requires clear disclosure of all terms and a straightforward cancellation mechanism.

## Cancellation fees are hidden behind fine print

Adobe transitioned to a subscription model in 2012, requiring users to pay regularly for access to its software, including popular products like Photoshop and Acrobat.

FTC's complaint details how Adobe steers consumers towards its "annual paid monthly" subscription plan without adequately informing them about the ETF, which can be as much as 50 percent of the remaining monthly payments if canceled within the first year.[[3]](#cite-adobe-3)

This fee is often hidden in fine print or behind small icons on Adobe's website. Consumers reported to FTC and the Better Business Bureau that they were unaware of the ETF or the requirement to keep the subscription for a year. Adobe's failure to disclose these terms clearly is central to FTC's allegations.

## Deceptive practices when users decide to cancel their subscriptions

The complaint also describes Adobe's cancellation process as intentionally complex, designed to deter consumers from canceling their subscriptions.

When attempting to cancel, consumers must navigate through multiple pages on Adobe's website, starting with locating the account management page, clicking on "Manage Plan," and then selecting "Cancel Your Plan."

Even after reaching this point, users are often forced to re-enter their password and complete a mandatory feedback page that prominently displays the ETF, effectively discouraging cancellation.

Furthermore, FTC alleges that Adobe's customer service adds to the difficulties by frequently dropping calls, disconnecting chats, and transferring customers between representatives, forcing them to re-explain their cancellation request each time. Consumers also reported continued billing despite believing they had canceled their subscriptions, further exacerbating their frustration.

## FTC seeks appropriate actions from Adobe

FTC's complaint seeks several forms of relief to address these issues. These include a permanent injunction to stop ongoing violations, monetary civil penalties for ROSCA violations, restitution for affected consumers, and the cancellation or modification of existing contracts entered into under deceptive terms.

The complaint also targets Adobe executives Sawhney, Senior Vice President of Digital Go To Market & Sales, and Wadhwani, President of Digital Media Business, accusing them of being aware of and continuing the unlawful practices.

Commission voted 3-0 to refer the civil penalty complaint to the Department of Justice (DOJ) for filing. The DOJ then filed the complaint, which will be decided by the court.

## Adobe denies the allegations

In response to FTC's action, Adobe has disputed the allegations. Dana Rao, Adobe's General Counsel and Chief Trust Officer, stated:[[4]](#cite-adobe-4)

> We are transparent with the terms and conditions of our subscription agreements and have a simple cancellation process. We will refute FTC's claims in court.

Adobe maintains that its subscription services are convenient, flexible, and cost-effective, allowing users to choose the plan that best fits their needs, timeline, and budget.

The lawsuit against Adobe highlights the broader regulatory scrutiny of subscription practices and consumer protection. The federal government began investigating Adobe's cancellation practices late last year, and this case is part of a larger effort to ensure companies do not use deceptive tactics to trap consumers in long-term subscriptions.

Adobe's recent attempt to acquire the product design platform Figma for $20 billion[[5]](#cite-the-verge-5) faced antitrust scrutiny, reflecting continued regulatory challenges for the company.[[6]](#cite-variety-6)

FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection Director Samuel Levine said that deceptive cancellation fees should stop being practiced, saying:

> Americans are tired of companies hiding the ball during subscription signup and then putting up roadblocks when they try to cancel. FTC will continue working to protect Americans from these illegal business practices.

## Frequently asked questions

Was Adobe sued by the FTC?

Yes. The FTC took action against Adobe and two executives in June 2024, alleging a hidden early termination fee and a hard cancellation process.{2} The case later ended in a proposed settlement that the Justice Department announced on March 13, 2026.{7}

How much is the Adobe settlement?

It is $150 million in total. The Justice Department says the proposed order requires $75 million in civil penalties and $75 million in free services for customers.{7} Adobe says it denies any wrongdoing.{8}

What is the Adobe hidden cancellation fee?

It is the early termination fee on the annual paid monthly plan. The FTC said it equals 50 percent of the remaining monthly payments if you cancel during the first year, and that Adobe buried it in fine print.{2}

What does the settlement require Adobe to do?

Adobe must give subscribers easy ways to cancel and clearly disclose any early termination fee and how it is calculated before enrolling them. For free trials longer than seven days, it must also send a reminder before the paid plan starts.{7}

What happened to the Adobe executives in the case?

The case named Maninder Sawhney and David Wadhwani, and the Justice Department says the proposed stipulated order is meant to resolve the case against Adobe and both employees.{7} We found no further detail on them.

Did Adobe admit wrongdoing?

No, not in the sources we read. Reuters quotes Adobe as saying it disagrees with the government's claims and denies any wrongdoing, while being pleased to resolve the matter.{8}

**Windows location service**. Microsoft’s location service helps determine the precise geographic location of your Windows device using a combination of GPS, nearby wireless access points and routers, cell towers, IP address, or default location.

Location services give you control over which apps are allowed to access your precise location. When location services are turned off, Windows and apps will not have access to device location, and some apps may not be able to access information about Wi-Fi networks. With location services turned on, apps can access approximate location and can request permission to use precise location. You can manage these permissions in Windows Settings. When location is enabled, data about cell towers and Wi-Fi access points and their locations are collected, de-identified, and used to improve location services. [Learn more about location in Windows](https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/p/?linkid=529987).

This location information can be viewed or deleted from your Microsoft account privacy dashboard.

There are some exceptions to how your device’s location can be determined that are not directly managed by the location settings. For example, desktop apps are a type of app that do not support per-app control over precise location access. Desktop apps are usually downloaded from the internet or installed from media (such as a CD, DVD, or USB storage device).

Even when you’ve turned off location services in Windows, some third-party apps and services could use other technologies (such as Bluetooth, IP address, cellular modem, etc.) or cloud-based location services to determine your device’s location with varying degrees of accuracy.

To facilitate getting help in an emergency, whenever you make an emergency call, Windows will attempt to determine and share your precise location, regardless of your location settings. You can turn off online speech recognition at any time and stop any apps that rely on the online speech recognition setting from sending your voice data to Microsoft. If you are using a HoloLens or Windows Mixed Reality headset, you can also turn off device-based speech recognition at any time. This will stop the device from listening for your voice input. [Learn more about speech recognition in Windows](https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/p/?linkid=2145715).

**Voice activation**. Windows provides supported apps with the ability to respond and take action based on voice keywords that are specific to that app.

Each app needs to ask for your permission before accessing your microphone. When a keyword is detected, the app will access and process your voice recording, take action, and respond, such as with a spoken answer. The app may send your voice recording to its own cloud services to process commands and collect the recordings for other purposes, such as improving its services.

Voice activation functionality can be enabled when the device is locked and the screen is off. Once an app is activated with a voice keyword, it may continue listening to the microphone. The app may be activated by anyone who speaks near the device and have access to the same set of capabilities and information as when the device is unlocked.

You can turn off voice activation at any time. [Learn more about voice activation in Windows](https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?linkid=874646).

Even when you’ve turned off voice activation, some third-party desktop apps and services could still be listening to the microphone and collect your voice input. [Learn more about third-party desktop apps and how they may still be able to access your microphone even with these settings turned off](https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/p/?linkid=2007461).

**Voice typing**. In Windows 11, dictation is now voice typing. Voice typing may use both device-based and online speech recognition technologies to power its speech-to-text transcription service. Recall is a Windows feature available exclusively on Copilot+ PCs that helps users find previously viewed content using remembered text or visual clues. To use Recall, users must opt-in to save snapshots — screen images with metadata like app name and time stamp — which are securely stored locally and protected with Windows Hello Enhanced Sign-in Security (ESS). Each time Recall is opened, users must authenticate using Windows Hello biometric sign-in or PIN to decrypt snapshot contents. Analysis and processing of snapshots occur only on the device. When you click on the microphone button inside the Search box within the Recall window, it enters what you said in the Search box. Recall securely stores all captured data—including personal data like snapshots, metadata, processing results, and user queries—locally on your Copilot+ PC and within your signed-in account. This information is never transmitted off your device unless you take action, such as copying a snapshot to another app or submitting feedback through the Windows Feedback Hub with a snapshot attached. The only way Recall content can be shared is by explicit user action on the device.

You can control your content (such as snapshots, metadata, search queries, and history) by pausing or deleting snapshots, filtering content, or using a supported browser in privacy mode. [Learn more about your privacy and control over your Recall experience](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/privacy-and-control-over-your-recall-experience-d404f672-7647-41e5-886c-a3c59680af15).

Recall also has a Sensitive Content filter that is on by default to help prevent the retention of information that might be more delicate in nature (e.g., credit card numbers, state issued ID numbers, etc.). Users can turn this filter off if they wish in Windows Settings.

# Nexus Breach Puts 153M IDs in Spy Crosshairs [2026]

![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/mbell.webp)

[Marcus Bell](https://shattered.io/author/mbell/)

Updated Sep 22, 2026 · 16 min read

The Nexus breach has already been framed as a fraud problem: 153 million driver’s licenses and 3 million travel documents for sale on a dark-web service, an FBI probe, and a company, IDScan.net, that has confirmed hackers pulled records out of its cloud. What has gotten less attention is a second, harder question raised directly by a September 14, 2026 analysis in **Lawfare**, titled “America’s Driver’s License Breach Is a National Security Disaster”: what happens when a foreign intelligence service, not a credit-card fraudster, gets the data first.

That distinction matters because driver’s licenses aren’t just payment-fraud bait. They’re the backbone of identity verification across banking, air travel, government facility access, and increasingly, AI-driven KYC (know-your-customer) systems. A stolen credit card gets canceled. A driver’s license number, tied to a face, a home address, and a document format that thousands of verification systems trust by default, doesn’t expire the same way. Below, we walk through the counterintelligence angle of the Nexus breach, why 153 million records changes the threat model rather than just the headline number, and what the absence of a coordinated federal security response signals about the state of critical infrastructure protection nine months into the incident’s public life.

## What Lawfare’s National Security Analysis Actually Argues

Lawfare’s framing departs from most of the coverage that followed the Nexus dark-web listing. Most outlets, understandably, led with scale: 153 million driver’s licenses tied to U.S. and Canadian citizens, plus 3 million travel documents, offered for sale through a service calling itself Nexus. Lawfare’s piece, published September 14, 2026, argues that treating this purely as a consumer-fraud event undercounts the real exposure. In the piece’s own words, the breach “is a huge breach that not only will be used for run-of-the-mill cybercrime but also will feed the intelligence machines of America’s adversaries.”

The core of that argument is straightforward once you separate the two buyer profiles for stolen ID data. A criminal marketplace buyer wants volume: enough license numbers and photos to open fraudulent accounts at scale before banks catch on. A state intelligence service wants something different, precision. It wants a clean, government-issued identity document, tied to a real address history and a real face, that it can use to build a cover identity, apply for access badges, or verify a synthetic persona against systems that were never designed to detect a forged-but-technically-real document. Lawfare’s analysis states plainly that licenses and identity documents “can be used to facilitate identity theft and phishing attacks, but because the data can be used to inform intelligence operations, an incident like this also has national security implications.” Read the full analysis at [Lawfare](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/america's-drivers-licence-breach-is-a-national-security-disaster).

That’s the pivot this article focuses on: not whether Nexus is real (the FBI’s involvement and IDScan.net’s own confirmation settle that), but what a dataset of this size and quality means once it’s in the hands of someone building long-term access rather than a quick score.

## The Confirmed Facts, and Where the Record Actually Stops

Before going further into the security implications, it’s worth being precise about what is actually confirmed versus what remains a claim by the seller. According to reporting cited by Lawfare and corroborated elsewhere, a dark-web service branding itself Nexus is advertising 153 million driver’s licenses belonging to U.S. and Canadian citizens, along with 3 million travel documents. Those figures are claims made by the Nexus operators themselves, not numbers independently verified against a single confirmed source system. The story was first broken by Brian Krebs at [KrebsOnSecurity](https://krebsonsecurity.com/), whose reporting on identity-theft marketplaces has a long track record of surfacing breaches well before affected companies acknowledge them publicly.

On the investigative side, the FBI has confirmed it is looking into a possible breach involving tens of millions of driver’s licenses belonging to people in the United States and Canada. The bureau’s New Orleans field office opened a formal investigation on September 1, 2026, after the Nexus service began selling the scans. An FBI spokesperson told Bloomberg News that the bureau is investigating a potential breach at an ID verification company that may have exposed scans of millions of Americans’ driver’s licenses.

Separately, [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/) reports that a Louisiana-based ID verification company, IDScan.net, has confirmed a data breach in which hackers stole driver’s licenses from the company’s cloud infrastructure. IDScan’s own breach notice lists full names, driver’s license numbers, and identity numbers from other government-issued documents including passports as compromised. What is not yet publicly and independently confirmed is a precise, verified link between the full 153-million-record Nexus claim and the IDScan.net breach specifically, that connection currently rests on investigative and journalistic analysis rather than an official joint attribution. Readers should treat the exact scale, and the precise chain of custody of the data, as still developing rather than closed.

## Why Driver’s License Data Is a Different Kind of Asset

Security teams have spent a decade building fraud models around payment card data and Social Security numbers. Driver’s license breaches historically got filed under “identity theft,” a category with well-understood remediation: credit freezes, fraud alerts, monitoring services. That playbook assumes the attacker’s goal is financial extraction. It breaks down when the attacker’s goal is persistent access.

Consider what a driver’s license actually proves to the systems that check it. It proves a name matches a face, an address is current enough to pass a soft verification, and a document format is recognized by whatever scanner or human is checking it. Airports use it for domestic travel under REAL ID rules. Banks use it to open accounts and clear KYC checks. Employers use it for I-9 verification. Federal contractors and cleared facilities use license and passport data as a baseline layer before deeper vetting kicks in. None of those systems were built to detect a real document number, paired with a real photo and a real address history, being used by someone who isn’t the person it was issued to. That’s precisely the gap Lawfare’s analysis is pointing at: a breach at this scale doesn’t just enable fraud, it potentially hands an adversary the raw material to build identities that pass first-layer scrutiny almost everywhere.

Reuters’ reporting on the FBI investigation adds a specific thread here. A source cited in Reuters’ coverage of the bureau’s inquiry described the exposure as creating legitimate national security risk for high-profile individuals specifically, the population most likely to be targeted for the kind of long-horizon intelligence operations Lawfare describes, rather than for the kind of one-off fraud most breach victims face.

## Table: How Nexus Compares to Prior Large-Scale ID Breaches

Scale alone doesn’t tell the full story, but it helps to place Nexus against other identity-document incidents that made national headlines in recent years. The table below uses only the publicly reported, named figures for each incident. Where a number is a seller’s claim rather than an independently confirmed figure, that is noted.

| Incident | Records Claimed/Confirmed | Document Type | Attribution Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nexus / IDScan.net (2026) | 153 million driver’s licenses; 3 million travel documents (Nexus seller claim) | Driver’s licenses, passports | FBI investigating; IDScan.net has confirmed a breach of its cloud environment |
| Florida DMV breach (2026) | Approx. 200,000 records reported | DMV records | Confirmed; disclosure timeline and single-login root cause separately reported |
| McKesson breach (2026) | Up to 284 million records claimed by ShinyHunters | Healthcare/identity data | Claimed by threat actor; company response ongoing |
| Manchester Airports Group breach (2026) | 8.7 million records reported | Traveler/identity data | Confirmed; ransom reportedly refused |

What stands out isn’t just that Nexus is larger than most comparable incidents, it’s that the document type sits closer to the “trusted verification credential” end of the spectrum than most breaches on this list. A healthcare record or a DMV record leaks personal details. A driver’s license or passport number leaks the credential itself.

## The Legal Backdrop: Why Selling This Data to Foreign Buyers Is Already Illegal

There’s an existing federal statute that speaks directly to the scenario Lawfare’s analysis raises, even though it wasn’t written with a breach like Nexus specifically in mind. Under U.S. data broker rules, it is unlawful for a data broker to sell, license, rent, trade, transfer, release, disclose, provide access to, or otherwise make available personally identifiable sensitive data of a United States individual to any foreign adversary country, or to any entity controlled by a foreign adversary. The same statute defines a government-issued identifier, explicitly including a Social Security number, passport number, or driver’s license number, as sensitive data covered by that prohibition. The [Federal Trade Commission](https://www.ftc.gov/), which shares enforcement authority over consumer data protection, has not announced any action tied to the Nexus data specifically as of this writing.

That statute governs data brokers, legitimate businesses that sell aggregated consumer data, not dark-web marketplaces operating outside any regulatory reach. Nexus doesn’t have to comply with a law written for licensed data brokers, and there’s no indication anyone involved intends to. But the statute is a useful marker of where Congress already drew the line on foreign-adversary access to exactly this category of data: names, addresses, and government identifiers. Nexus represents the scenario that law was designed to prevent, just executed through theft and dark-web resale instead of a commercial transaction.

## Market and Industry Impact: Identity Verification Vendors Under Pressure

The immediate commercial fallout lands on the identity-verification industry itself. IDScan.net sits in a market of vendors that banks, fintechs, car-rental companies, and age-verification services rely on to scan and validate government IDs in real time. If a vendor in that supply chain is confirmed as the breach source, every downstream customer inherits a version of the same question: was the document data we sent for verification also exposed, and can our verification pipeline still be trusted to catch a forged or stolen ID built from that same dataset?

That question compounds because ID-scanning vendors occupy an unusual trust position. Unlike a retailer that stores payment tokens, an ID-verification vendor’s entire business model depends on ingesting the most sensitive document data a customer has, the literal image and number of a government credential, and asserting that its handling of that data is secure enough to justify the access. A confirmed breach at that layer of the stack doesn’t just cost IDScan.net customers and legal exposure. It puts pressure on every competing vendor to demonstrate, publicly and quickly, that their own cloud storage and data retention practices don’t carry the same risk. Expect procurement teams at banks and fintechs to start asking pointed questions about data retention windows, encryption-at-rest practices, and whether raw document images are ever kept longer than the verification transaction requires.

There’s a second-order effect worth watching too. Companies that rely on ID scans for age verification, a category that has expanded fast under 2025 and 2026 state-level age-verification laws for social media and adult content, are exactly the kind of high-volume, lower-security-maturity customers that tend to get breached next. If Nexus-style data becomes a template for what’s achievable against ID-verification vendors, expect regulators and plaintiffs’ attorneys to start treating “we outsourced ID verification to a third party” as a liability question rather than a compliance checkbox.

## The Enforcement Gap: Why No Agency Has Stepped In Yet

One of the more striking parts of this story, two weeks after the FBI investigation opened, is the absence of a visible enforcement or coordination response from the agencies that would normally own this kind of national-security-adjacent breach. The FTC hasn’t announced an action. State attorneys general haven’t coordinated a joint response despite the multi-state scope of the exposed records. There’s no public indication yet of a CISA advisory specific to Nexus or IDScan.net, even though CISA has been active elsewhere in 2026, adding a steady stream of new CVEs to its [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog) under the accelerated disclosure timelines set by Binding Operational Directive 26-04.

That gap matters more for a national-security framing than a consumer-fraud one. Consumer-fraud breaches eventually get a regulatory response because there’s a clear injured party and a clear financial harm to quantify: fraudulent charges, credit damage, out-of-pocket costs. A counterintelligence risk doesn’t produce that kind of immediately measurable harm. It produces a slower, harder-to-attribute risk: an intelligence officer using a stolen identity to apply for a job at a defense contractor, or to establish a years-long cover identity that never triggers a fraud alert because no fraudulent charge is ever made. Agencies built to respond to financial harm don’t have an obvious lane for that threat model, and that’s arguably the structural problem Lawfare’s analysis is describing without naming it directly.

## Historical Context: From Equifax to OPM to Nexus

This isn’t the first time a large identity-data breach has raised a national-security question rather than just a consumer-fraud one. The 2015 Office of Personnel Management breach, which exposed security-clearance background investigation files on more than 21 million people, was widely assessed by U.S. intelligence officials as a foreign intelligence-collection operation rather than a financial-crime one, precisely because the data (family relationships, financial history, foreign contacts) was far more useful for recruiting or blackmail than for fraud. The 2017 Equifax breach, by contrast, exposed roughly 147 million Americans’ Social Security numbers and was treated almost entirely as a consumer-fraud and credit-protection story, even though the scale rivaled what intelligence services would find useful.

Nexus sits closer to the OPM model than the Equifax one, both in the kind of data involved (identity documents rather than just numbers) and in the emerging framing from outlets like Lawfare. The difference is that OPM was a breach of a government system, which triggered an automatic national-security review process. Nexus, if the IDScan.net attribution holds, is a breach of a private vendor, which means the national-security review process that kicked in automatically for OPM doesn’t have an obvious equivalent trigger here. That’s a structural gap, not a partisan one, and it’s likely to be the actual policy debate that follows this story once the initial breach-notification cycle winds down.

## Competitive Landscape: How ID-Verification Vendors Stack Up on Security Posture

With IDScan.net now the named vendor at the center of a breach of this size, customers and competitors across the identity-verification space are being forced into comparison mode. The table below summarizes how the broader category is typically evaluated on security posture, based on publicly available vendor security documentation and disclosure practices, not on any claim that a specific competitor has been breached.

| Evaluation Criteria | Why It Matters After Nexus | What Buyers Should Ask Vendors Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Document retention window | Long retention of raw scans increases breach blast radius | How long are scanned document images stored after verification completes? |
| Cloud storage encryption | IDScan.net’s stolen data reportedly came from cloud infrastructure | Is document data encrypted at rest with customer-managed keys? |
| Third-party breach notification SLA | Downstream customers need fast notice to reassess exposure | What is the contractual notification window after a confirmed incident? |
| Data minimization practices | Fewer fields stored means less usable data if breached | Does the vendor store full document images or only extracted fields? |
| Independent security audits | Self-attestation isn’t sufficient for a vendor holding government IDs | Is there a current SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certification? |

None of this is a claim that any named competitor has a worse security posture than IDScan.net, there’s no public evidence to support that either way. It’s a reflection of the questions the entire category is now facing from customers who, before September 2026, likely never asked their ID-verification vendor a single question about cloud storage architecture.

## What Happens to the Data From Here

Once identity-document data is listed on a service like Nexus, the buyer pool splits fast. Some of it will move through familiar cybercrime channels, funding account-takeover fraud, synthetic-identity credit applications, and SIM-swap attacks that use license data to pass carrier verification. That portion is well understood and, while damaging, has established remediation paths through credit freezes and fraud monitoring.

The portion Lawfare’s analysis is flagging is the slice that never surfaces in a fraud-monitoring dashboard at all. A foreign intelligence service doesn’t need to buy the entire 153-million-record set. It needs a small, curated subset, ideally identities matching a specific demographic or geographic profile useful for building long-term cover, and it can acquire that subset quietly, use it slowly, and never trigger the kind of transaction pattern that flags a breach victim’s identity as compromised. That’s the piece of this story that doesn’t have a clean metric, a dollar figure, or a breach-notification letter attached to it, and it’s precisely why it’s the hardest part of the story to act on.

## Predictions: Where This Story Goes Next

* **Expect a congressional inquiry before a coordinated agency response.** The scale and the foreign-adversary angle make this a likely candidate for hearing requests from Senate and House committees with data-privacy or intelligence jurisdiction, even if no formal FTC or CISA action follows quickly.
* **ID-verification vendors will accelerate security disclosures.** Competitors to IDScan.net have a strong incentive to publicly differentiate on data retention and encryption practices in the coming months, whether or not regulators force it.
* **Civil litigation will outpace regulatory action.** Given the pattern already visible in other 2026 breaches, expect the lawsuits already filed against IDScan.net to expand, with plaintiffs’ attorneys leaning on the national-security framing to argue for higher damages.
* **REAL ID and airport-adjacent identity checks face renewed scrutiny.** Any incident tying stolen license data to a security-relevant access failure, even a single documented case, would likely trigger a broader review of how airports and federal facilities validate identity documents against breach databases.
* **The attribution question stays unresolved for months, not weeks.** Tying the full 153-million-record Nexus claim definitively to IDScan.net, or ruling out additional source systems, is the kind of forensic work that typically takes quarters, not days, especially with an active FBI investigation limiting public disclosure.

## What Individuals and Security Teams Can Actually Do

For individuals, the practical advice hasn’t changed much from any large identity-document breach: place a credit freeze with all three bureaus, watch for unfamiliar account-opening notifications, and treat any unexpected verification request tied to your name or address with more suspicion than usual. Driver’s license numbers can’t be reissued as easily as a credit card, so the exposure window is effectively indefinite unless your state DMV offers a number-reissuance path, which most don’t as a routine service.

For security teams at organizations that rely on third-party ID verification, this is a reasonable moment to audit exactly what data your verification vendor stores, for how long, and under what encryption standard, rather than assuming a signed contract covers the risk. It’s also worth mapping which of your own KYC or access-control processes rely purely on document validity rather than a second, independent signal (device fingerprinting, behavioral biometrics, liveness detection), since document-only verification is exactly the layer a dataset like Nexus is built to defeat.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the Nexus breach, in simple terms?

Nexus is the name of a dark-web service that began advertising 153 million driver’s licenses and 3 million travel documents belonging to U.S. and Canadian citizens for sale. The FBI opened a formal investigation on September 1, 2026, and IDScan.net, a Louisiana-based ID-verification company, has confirmed hackers stole driver’s license data from its cloud environment.

### Why is this being called a national security issue instead of just a data breach?

Lawfare’s September 14, 2026 analysis argues that government-issued identity documents are useful to foreign intelligence services for building cover identities and supporting long-term operations, not just to cybercriminals for fraud. That dual-use risk is what separates this breach’s framing from a typical consumer-data incident.

### Is the 153 million figure confirmed?

The 153 million driver’s licenses and 3 million travel documents figures are claims made by the Nexus service itself. They have not been independently verified against a single confirmed source system, though the FBI investigation and IDScan.net’s own breach confirmation both lend credibility to the broader story.

### Has any regulator taken action yet?

As of September 15, 2026, there is no public indication of FTC or state attorney general enforcement action specific to this breach. The FBI’s investigation, opened September 1, 2026, remains the primary confirmed federal response.

### Is it illegal to sell this kind of data to a foreign government?

Yes, under existing U.S. data broker rules, it is unlawful for a data broker to sell sensitive personal data, including driver’s license numbers and passport numbers, to a foreign adversary country or an entity it controls. That statute governs licensed data brokers rather than dark-web marketplaces, but it establishes the legal baseline for why this kind of exposure is treated as a security issue.

### What should someone do if their driver’s license may be part of this breach?

Place a credit freeze with all three major credit bureaus, monitor for unfamiliar account-opening activity, and contact your state DMV to ask about options if you suspect your license number specifically has been compromised. Unlike a credit card, a driver’s license number generally can’t be quickly canceled and reissued.

### How does this compare to the 2015 OPM breach?

The 2015 OPM breach exposed security-clearance background files on more than 21 million people and was widely assessed as a foreign intelligence-collection operation. Nexus involves a much larger volume of records but from a private vendor rather than a government system, which means it doesn’t automatically trigger the same national-security review process that a breach of a federal system does.

## **How the fake Facebook Marketplace listing works**

Malwarebytes analyzed an example sent through iMessage. The text asked whether an item was still available and included an image resembling a Facebook Marketplace listing. The clever part appears when you look at the supposed seller. The recipient's real name is there.

However, Malwarebytes noticed something strange. The profile photo did not belong to the recipient. Researchers traced the picture to another Facebook user who happened to have the same name.

That suggests the scammer may have started with a name and matching phone number. Those details could potentially come from breached data or another source. The attacker could then use the name to build a convincing fake Marketplace screenshot. Seeing your name creates an obvious question: "Is someone pretending to be me?" Before you know it, you're typing a reply.

## **Why scammers want you to respond**

This technique is known as a conversation lure. Instead of immediately asking for a password or sending an obvious phishing link, the sender gives you a reason to start talking. In this case, the lure feels personal. Someone apparently [put your name](https://www.foxnews.com/tech/what-scammer-sees-moment-you-google-your-name) on a Marketplace listing. You may want to correct the buyer or find out what happened. You might also worry that someone has created a fake Facebook account in your name.

The exact motive behind this particular campaign remains unclear because determining the next step would require engaging with the sender. Still, replying to suspicious texts carries its own risk. The Federal Trade Commission warns that even replying to an unexpected text can confirm that a scammer has reached a working telephone number. That could lead to more scam calls and texts.

## **Your reply may tell scammers more than you realize**

Think about how harmless a response such as "wrong person" feels. You haven't shared a password or sent money. You haven't clicked a suspicious website. However, you've given the sender something useful: confirmation that someone is actively using the number and willing to respond. Malwarebytes reports that a live number can become more valuable to scammers and potentially be resold to others. The number could also be combined with additional information gathered from public profiles, breached databases or other sources. That can help set up another scam.

You might later receive a fake delivery alert. Another message could pretend to come from your bank. A scammer might eventually try to steal a verification code, direct you to a malicious site or build a longer conversation designed to gain your trust. We recently looked at [what a scammer can do with your name, phone number and address.](https://www.foxnews.com/tech/scammer-has-your-name-phone-number-address-what-can-they-do) Those details can become far more useful when criminals combine them with other personal information.

## **How AI could make personalized scams easier to scale**

Creating individual Marketplace screenshots for thousands of people once would have required a lot of tedious work. AI and automation can change that equation. Malwarebytes says an attacker with a list containing names and phone numbers could potentially use an AI agent to help create personalized lures at scale. However, researchers have not established that AI created the specific example they examined. Still, automation makes this kind of personalization much easier to produce.

That's an important shift in how we should judge suspicious messages. A text knowing your name provides little reassurance that the sender actually knows you. Personal information gets exposed through [breaches](https://www.foxnews.com/tech/what-exactly-data-breach-why-should-i-care), scraped from public sources and traded in criminal marketplaces. Once scammers connect a few pieces, they can make a random message feel surprisingly personal.

## **Does this mean your Facebook account was hacked?**

No. Seeing your name on one of these fake Marketplace images does not, by itself, mean someone has accessed your Facebook account. The Marketplace screenshot may simply be fabricated. That's why I would resist the urge to reply to the sender asking what's going on. Instead, check Facebook yourself.

## **What Apple says about suspicious iMessages**

Apple says this type of deceptive messaging uses social engineering, a tactic in which scammers rely on impersonation and manipulation to persuade people to share personal information. Criminals may pretend to represent a trusted company or organization while trying to obtain passwords, security codes or financial details.

Apple also points to an important iMessage protection. By default, users cannot open links sent by an unknown iMessage sender until they add that person to their contacts or reply to the message. That gives you another reason to avoid responding to an unexpected text. Apple recommends treating suspicious, unexpected messages as potential scams and contacting the company directly through a trusted channel. The company also says users can filter unknown senders, report suspicious messages and block unwanted contacts through Messages.

## **How to protect yourself from scam texts on iPhone**

Apple's Messages app includes tools to help [filter unwanted texts](https://www.foxnews.com/tech/anti-scam-settings-iphone-pixel-galaxy-check), report suspicious messages and block senders. Since this Facebook Marketplace scam arrives through iMessage, here's how to use those protections on an iPhone.

### **Turn on screening for unknown senders**

Messages from unknown senders will appear in a separate folder instead of your main conversation list. Apple says you won't receive notifications for these messages unless you've chosen to allow certain categories of unknown messages.

### **Report a suspicious iMessage**

Apple says reporting an iMessage sends the sender's information and message content to Apple. The message is then permanently deleted from your iPhone. However, reporting does not automatically block the sender, so follow the blocking steps below. If you have already replied, the reporting option may no longer be available. For SMS, MMS or RCS messages that don't display a reporting option, [Apple recommends](https://www.foxnews.com/category/tech/companies/apple) contacting your wireless carrier directly.

### **Block the scammer's number**

Blocking prevents messages from that number from reaching you. The sender won't receive a notification that you've blocked them.

### **Check messages Apple has flagged as spam**

**Important:** These protections can reduce exposure to scam messages, but they cannot guarantee that every personalized phishing attempt will be detected. Don't reply to a suspicious Marketplace message simply because it contains your real name.

## **How to stay safe from fake Facebook Marketplace texts**

A message like this is designed to make you react. Instead, give yourself a moment and investigate through channels you trust.

### **1) Don't reply to the text**

Even telling the sender they have the wrong person can confirm that somebody is actively using the number. The FTC recommends avoiding replies to unexpected messages from unknown numbers.

### **2) Don't use links or contact information in the message**

[Don't click a link](https://www.foxnews.com/tech/scam-text-test-spot-danger-before-you-tap), call a number or scan a QR code supplied in the conversation. Never send the person a one-time security code or a screenshot containing security information. If you need to check Facebook, open the app yourself or type the address directly into your browser.

### **3) Use strong antivirus software**

Strong antivirus software can help protect you if a scammer eventually sends a malicious link or tries to get you to download malware. It can also warn you about some dangerous websites before they cause trouble. ### **4) Check your Facebook account independently**

Open Facebook and review your Marketplace activity and messages. Look for anything you didn't post or send. You should also review your [account security](https://www.foxnews.com/category/tech/topics/security) for unfamiliar logins, changed contact information or other activity you don't recognize.

### **5) Check with a known sender another way**

If a suspicious message appears to come from someone you actually know, contact that person through a different method. For example, call a number you already have saved rather than using contact information supplied in the suspicious message.

### **6) Report and block suspicious texts**

On an iPhone, follow the reporting and blocking steps above. Android users can use their messaging app's built-in spam reporting and blocking features. The FTC also recommends forwarding unwanted texts to 7726 (SPAM). These reports can help wireless providers identify and block similar messages.

### **7) Report a Facebook impersonator**

If you discover that someone really has created a Facebook profile pretending to be you, preserve the profile's URL and report it to Facebook. A fake screenshot alone does not prove that an impersonating Facebook profile actually exists. Check Facebook independently before assuming someone has created one.

### **8) Secure your Facebook account if something looks wrong**

If you discover an unfamiliar login, changed account information or other evidence of unauthorized access, start Facebook's account recovery process immediately. You should also review your password and enable two-factor authentication ([2FA](https://www.foxnews.com/tech/what-two-factor-authentication-should-enable-it)). Facebook currently places its two-factor authentication controls under **Accounts Center > Password and security > Two-factor authentication**.

### **9) Reduce the personal information scammers can find**

This scam shows why [exposed personal information](https://www.foxnews.com/tech/scammers-build-profile-using-data-brokers) can be so useful to criminals. Your name and phone number may already appear on people-search sites or in data-broker databases. Removing that information won't erase data already exposed in a breach, but it can reduce what scammers can easily find and use to personalize future attacks. ## **What if you already replied?**

Don't assume a single response means your phone or Facebook account has been compromised. A reply alone does not give someone access to your Facebook account. What you should do next depends on how far the interaction went.

## **Kurt's key takeaways**

What makes this scam so convincing is the personal detail. You see your own name on a Marketplace listing you never created, and of course you want to know what's going on. That's exactly why you should avoid replying to the stranger who sent it.

Instead, open Facebook yourself and check your account. If you don't see the listing or any suspicious activity, report the text, block the sender and move on. If something looks wrong, secure your Facebook account right away.

The bigger concern here is how easily scammers can use pieces of our personal information to make a random text feel legitimate. Your name and phone number may already be available through a data breach, data broker or another source. Seeing accurate information about yourself in an unexpected message should make you more cautious, not more trusting.
